claim: Among 1,153 web-based digital platform workers across 21 Latin American and Caribbean countries, mean hourly pay was US$5.48 while the median was US$2.57, meaning the average is 2.13 times the median and describes almost nobody's actual earnings.
stance_target: The position that platform and creator income distributions are so right-skewed that mean earnings figures are structurally misleading and only medians should be reported
scope_conditions: 21 Latin American and Caribbean countries; n = 1,153 web-based digital platform workers; ILO Regional Office for Latin America and the Caribbean, published 2025; freelancing and microwork tasks (database research, surveys, graphic design), not content creation; LAC not Southeast Asia
quoted_support: The average hourly pay for workers surveyed is 5.48 United States dollars (USD), and the median is USD 2.57.

claim: Median income from platform work alone is roughly equal to the national minimum wage, while workers who also hold non-platform work have median incomes at least double the minimum wage, so platform income only clears a living wage when it is not the sole source.
stance_target: The position that platform-only income rarely constitutes a living wage and adequacy depends on holding other work
scope_conditions: Selected LAC countries analysed within the 1,153-worker survey; 2025; ratio computed against national minimum wages
quoted_support: when considering only the median income from digital platform work, the ratio to the national minimum wage is closer to one, indicating that these payments are closer to the minimum wage.
numbers: at least 2x minimum wage for those with other work
52 percent say platform work is not primary income

claim: Workers who work exclusively on web-based platforms became less formally employed after entry: 38.9 percent identified as formal workers in the three months before joining, but only 17.7 percent describe their current platform job as formal work.
stance_target: The position that entering full-time platform work is associated with a measured downgrade in employment formality rather than an upgrade
scope_conditions: Subsample of the n = 1,153 survey who work exclusively on web-based platforms; self-reported retrospective status; LAC, 21 countries, 2025
quoted_support: they were asked about their work status up to three months before they started working on these platforms and, of these, 38.9 percent identified themselves as formal workers.

claim: When platform workers name the risks of their work, financial insecurity leads at 13 percent, followed by internet connection problems at 11 percent and lack of growth opportunities at 10 percent, with no single reason approaching a majority.
stance_target: The position that stated reasons for dissatisfaction or exit in platform work are diffuse rather than concentrated on one dominant cause
scope_conditions: n = 1,153 web-based platform workers, 21 LAC countries, 2025; these are self-reported risks, NOT reasons given by people who actually quit, so they cannot stand in for exit reasons without qualification
quoted_support: These include financial insecurity (13 percent), internet connection issues (11 percent) and lack of growth opportunities (10 percent).

claim: Platform workers report working at least ten hours a day across six and a half days a week and nearly 11 nights a month, and about 40 percent are excluded from health care and social security coverage.
stance_target: The position that platform income is earned at hour counts well above standard full-time and without social protection, so hourly comparisons to salaried work understate the gap
scope_conditions: n = 1,153 web-based platform workers, 21 LAC countries, 2025; night work defined as 10pm-5am; the report notes coverage where it exists may attach to a traditional main job rather than to platform work
quoted_support: on average, respondents work at least ten hours a day, six and a half days a month, and almost 11 days at night (from 10 p.m. to 5 a.m.).
numbers: 29 percent work up to five days/week
40 percent excluded from health and social security
